cards.title: Near-linear-query reconstruction of bounded-degree graphs
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(\Delta\geq2\), is there a randomized exact reconstruction algorithm \(A_{\Delta}\) and constants \(C_{\Delta}>0\), \(k_{\Delta}\geq0\) such that every hidden connected simple unweighted undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) labeled vertices with maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) can be reconstructed using \[\mathbb E[Q(A_{\Delta},G)]\leq C_{\Delta}\,n(\log(n+2))^{k_{\Delta}}\] queries to an oracle that returns the shortest-path distance between one requested pair of vertices?

source_formulation.text: Thus the open question from [27] of whether general graphs of bounded degree can be reconstructed using \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n)\) distance queries remains open and answering it […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 5

cards.why: The problem asks how much pairwise distance information is inherently needed to discover an entire sparse network. A near-linear worst-input guarantee would show that distances allow almost output-sized exact reconstruction despite hiding every edge, without relying on randomness in the network itself.
cards.status_note: Read the original complete query model, theorem guarantees and open-question remark. Checked the March 2026 treelength theorem and the full SWAT 2026 graph-reconstruction section. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no near-linear expected distance-query algorithm for every connected graph of fixed maximum degree. The source’s expectation convention is retained as exact randomized reconstruction, not a random-input or stronger all-distances model.

progress.text: The source reaches near-linear expected queries on random regular graphs and retains the general bounded-degree question.
A full preprint gives deterministic linearithmic queries with a bounded-treelength promise.
The SWAT paper adds deterministic subquadratic reconstruction for bounded cutwidth and restates the general three-halves-exponent upper bound.

sentences: All vertices of a connected bounded-degree graph are known, but its edges are hidden.
One query returns only the shortest-path distance between two named vertices.
The goal is to recover every edge using a linear number of vertices times polylogarithmically many expected queries.
The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for each fixed graph, and the returned answer must be exact.
Near-linear results for random regular or bounded-treelength graphs do not cover every graph in the question.

cards.definitions:
The algorithm is given the entire vertex set, identified with \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the fixed degree bound. The edge set is hidden. The graph is fixed throughout the execution and is promised connected; no random input distribution is assumed.

A query supplies two named vertices \(u,v\) and receives the integer
\[d_{G}(u,v)=\min\{\text{number of edges on a path from }u\text{ to }v\}.\]
The answer contains no path, intermediate vertices or distances to other destinations. An edge has distance one. Computing all distances from one vertex by querying this oracle costs \(n-1\) queries, rather than one query.

The algorithm may choose each new query using all previous answers and its private random bits. Its output must be exactly the set \(E(G)\) on the given vertex labels. Isomorphism type, an approximate metric, a graph consistent with only some answers, or a sample of edges is insufficient.

The randomized convention is Las Vegas: the output is correct whenever returned, and the procedure terminates with probability one. The query bound is an expectation over its internal randomness for each fixed allowed graph. This is not average-case complexity over randomly generated graphs. Deterministic algorithms also qualify.

The constants may depend on the fixed \(\Delta\), but not on \(n\) or the particular graph. The displayed bound specifies the meaning of \(\widetilde O(n)\): a linear number of vertices times a fixed power of a logarithm. A bound \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) does not meet it.

Only calls to the distance oracle are charged in this query-complexity question. The algorithm must be an effective finite procedure, but no separate polynomial bound on local computation or memory is imposed. No restriction is placed on the number of adaptive rounds. There is no additional promise of bounded treewidth, treelength, cutwidth or a planar graph.

Simplicity matters because distances cannot reveal edge multiplicities or loops. Connectedness is also part of the source model: allowing a graph with just one hidden edge and otherwise isolated vertices would already force a quadratic search for that edge.
cards.answer_criterion: Give algorithms with the displayed expected-query bound for every fixed degree bound, and prove exact reconstruction on every promised graph, or show that such bounds are impossible for at least one fixed degree bound. A lower bound against the source’s particular algorithm alone does not refute the general question.

context_blocks.title: A general upper bound still has a polynomial gap
context_blocks.text: The original source compares its algorithm with the earlier \(\widetilde O_{\Delta}(n^{3/2})\)-expected-query reconstruction algorithm. The 2026 SWAT paper still identifies this as the best known general bound for connected bounded-degree graphs.

context_blocks.title: The source obtains the target on random regular graphs
context_blocks.text: The source’s Theorem 1 gives \(\widetilde O(n)\) expected distance queries for uniformly random regular graphs of fixed degree. Its general-graph guarantee is weaker. The random-graph theorem averages over a restricted input distribution and therefore does not establish the per-graph bound asked here.

context_blocks.title: The source algorithm itself cannot solve the full question
context_blocks.text: The concluding remark gives complete binary trees as a family requiring a superlinear number of queries for the particular Simple algorithm. That limitation does not apply to every possible reconstruction algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Recent near-linear results require additional structure
context_blocks.text: Kaudan and Nayyeri give deterministic \(O_{\Delta,\tau}(n\log n)\) reconstruction for graphs with bounded treelength and a supplied bound \(\tau\). Treelength means the minimum, over tree decompositions, of the largest graph-metric distance between vertices in one bag. The 2026 SWAT result instead gives deterministic subquadratic reconstruction for bounded cutwidth. Neither hypothesis follows from bounded degree alone.

cards.context:
The original source compares its algorithm with the earlier \(\widetilde O_{\Delta}(n^{3/2})\)-expected-query reconstruction algorithm. The 2026 SWAT paper still identifies this as the best known general bound for connected bounded-degree graphs.

The source’s Theorem 1 gives \(\widetilde O(n)\) expected distance queries for uniformly random regular graphs of fixed degree. Its general-graph guarantee is weaker. The random-graph theorem averages over a restricted input distribution and therefore does not establish the per-graph bound asked here.

The concluding remark gives complete binary trees as a family requiring a superlinear number of queries for the particular Simple algorithm. That limitation does not apply to every possible reconstruction algorithm.

Kaudan and Nayyeri give deterministic \(O_{\Delta,\tau}(n\log n)\) reconstruction for graphs with bounded treelength and a supplied bound \(\tau\). Treelength means the minimum, over tree decompositions, of the largest graph-metric distance between vertices in one bag. The 2026 SWAT result instead gives deterministic subquadratic reconstruction for bounded cutwidth. Neither hypothesis follows from bounded degree alone.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
